question:
A previously healthy 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of blisters and redness on his neck and chest for 2 days. He has also had a fever. He is lethargic and has not eaten well since the rash appeared. He has not had coughing, wheezing, or dysuria. He is an only child and there is no family history of serious illness. His immunizations are up-to-date. His temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 90/min, and blood pressure is 80/40 mm Hg. Examination shows flaccid blisters over his neck and trunk that rupture easily. Areas of erythematous moist skin are also noted. Twirling an eraser over the trunk results in a blister. Oropharyngeal examination is normal. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 12 g/dL
Leukocyte count 22,000/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 77%
Eosinophils 3%
Lymphocytes 18%
Monocytes 2%
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 60 mm/h
Urinalysis is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Flaccid blisters over neck and trunk that rupture easily" -> "Erythematous moist skin noted" -> "Blister formation with eraser twirling" -> "Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome presentation" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Lethargy and poor appetite" -> "Fever (38.9°C)" -> "Systemic illness" -> "Toxic epidermal necrolysis less likely" -> 60%
enhanced_information: The presentation of flaccid blisters over the neck and trunk that rupture easily, along with erythematous moist skin and blister formation with eraser twirling, is highly suggestive of Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. The leukocytosis with a high percentage of segmented neutrophils further supports this diagnosis. The presence of lethargy, poor appetite, and fever does not align with toxic epidermal necrolysis, making it less likely. No evidence from the retrieved paths significantly impacts the diagnosis.
analysis: The clinical presentation of flaccid blisters that rupture easily, along with erythematous moist skin and positive Nikolsky sign (blister formation with eraser twirling), is highly indicative of Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. The leukocytosis with a high percentage of segmented neutrophils further supports this diagnosis. The absence of mucosal involvement and the lack of features typical of toxic epidermal necrolysis make it less likely. Scarlet fever typically presents with a sandpaper-like rash and is less likely in this case. Pemphigus vulgaris and bullous pemphigoid are autoimmune blistering disorders that do not typically present with the described clinical features. Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.
